hint1: You do this hundreds of times a day on a phone.

hint1: Every page on the web has its own one.

hint1: Most sites show it in the same place on every page.

hint4: A long strip of buttons leading to the main parts of a site.

hint1: Forms often use one to ask for your country.

hint1: Most shopping sites have one at the top.

hint4: Google's homepage is almost nothing but one of these.

hint1: Your phone's home screen is full of them.

hint1: You need one to apply for a passport.

hint1: A login screen has two of them.
hint2: Your password goes into one.
hint3: Click inside it and a line starts flashing.
hint4: The empty space where you enter your name or email.

hint1: Sign-up forms often have one near the end.

hint4: 'I have read the rules' usually has one beside it.

hint1: Blogs often show 'Popular posts' in one.

hint1: It makes a page more lively than text alone.

hint3: You can watch or listen without leaving the page.
hint4: A YouTube clip placed right on your own page.

hint1: Sports teams and pop stars both care about it.

hint1: Designers often collect its rules in a style guide.

hint4: Everything you can see that tells you which company it is.

hint1: Good designers check for it on every page.
hint2: Without it, a site feels messy and confusing.

hint4: 'Use one font everywhere to keep ___ across the site.'

hint1: Designers choose it before building anything.
hint2: WeChat's is mainly green, white and grey.
hint3: A site usually sticks to three to five main shades.
hint4: In art class, you mix shades on a board with this name.

hint1: It can make a page feel serious or playful.
hint2: Bold or thin, big or small, Arial or Georgia.
hint3: It includes the spacing between lines, not only size.
hint4: The art of choosing and arranging how writing looks.

hint1: Newspapers and printed novels often choose this kind of lettering.
hint2: Georgia and Garamond are well-known examples.
hint3: It can make writing look traditional and formal.
hint4: Tiny finishing strokes on the ends of each letter.

hint1: Most phone apps use this style of lettering.
hint2: Helvetica and Calibri are famous examples.
hint3: It looks clean and modern, so it suits screens.
hint4: The letters have no little finishing strokes at the ends.

hint1: Painters and photographers think about it a lot.
hint2: Grey writing on a grey background has very little.
hint3: Black next to white has the most.
hint4: 'Use strong ___ so the button stands out from the background.'

hint1: Apple's website uses lots of it to feel calm.
hint2: It gives a busy page room to breathe.
hint3: It can be any shade; it is just the unused area.
hint4: The clear areas around and between text and images.

hint1: Soldiers on parade show it perfectly.

hint3: A grid helps designers get it right.
hint4: 'Text can have left, centre or right ___.'

hint1: Every magazine cover and poster has one.
hint2: Big photo at the top, text underneath: that's one kind.
hint3: How the parts of a screen are set out together.
hint4: 'The new ___ puts the menu on the left and the photos on the right.'

hint1: Designers use an invisible one to keep a site neat.
hint2: A photo gallery often uses one: equal boxes across and down.
hint3: Instagram profiles show photos in one, three across.
hint4: Noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe) is played on a 3-by-3 one.

hint1: Newspapers use it to guide your eyes down a page.
hint2: A huge headline and tiny small print show it at work.
hint3: It decides what you notice straight away, what comes next, and what comes last.
hint4: Like a ranking of what matters most on the screen.

hint1: Visitors usually see it before they scroll at all.
hint2: Apple's main site shows a huge photo of its newest phone here.
hint3: A large photo, a short headline and one button, right under the header.
hint4: The eye-catching welcome section you meet first when a site opens.

hint1: Most adverts and shop websites end with one.
hint2: It tells the visitor exactly what to do next.
hint3: 'Start your free trial' and 'Get the app' are examples.
hint4: Words like 'Shop now!' that push visitors to do one thing.

hint1: Every website, advert and film has one in mind.
hint2: Designers choose colours and words to suit them.
hint3: For a toy shop website, it is children and their parents.
hint4: The answer to: 'Who exactly is this website made for?'

hint1: Most modern websites are built this way.
hint2: Turn a tablet sideways and the site rearranges itself neatly.
hint3: Three columns on a laptop become one column on a mobile.
hint4: One site that works well on every device, big or small.

hint1: Breaking one can confuse visitors.
hint2: Putting the logo in the top-left corner is one.
hint3: A shopping trolley icon at the top right is another.
hint4: A common habit across websites that everyone recognises at once.

hint1: Words and colours both help to create it.
hint2: A bank's site is serious; a toy shop's is playful.
hint3: A site's can be friendly, formal or funny.
hint4: 'Hey gamers!' sets a casual ___; 'Dear Sir' sets a formal one.

hint1: You judge this at the end of a design project.
hint2: Clear menus and a strong message can improve it.
hint3: If a charity site raises lots of money, this is high.
hint4: How well a website achieves its aim for its audience.

hint1: Big tech companies hire whole teams to improve it.
hint2: Slow loading, confusing menus and pop-ups all damage it.
hint3: It covers the emotions a visitor has from arrival to exit.
hint4: UI is how the screens look; this is how the whole visit goes.

hint1: Every app and game has one, good or bad.
hint2: WeChat's has four tabs along the bottom.
hint3: Menus, icons, sliders and tabs make it up.
hint4: UX is the whole visit; this is the part you see and tap.

hint1: Many governments require it on public websites.
hint2: Captions on videos for deaf visitors improve it.
hint3: Screen readers, zoomable text and alt text all support it.
hint4: Making a site work for visitors who can't see, hear or use a mouse.

hint1: Designers try to raise it with every update.
hint2: Tiny buttons and hidden menus make it worse.
hint3: Can a visitor buy something or find a page without getting stuck?
hint4: How quickly and smoothly visitors can get things done on a site.

hint1: Good apps are often described this way in reviews.
hint2: Swiping to the next photo is like this: even toddlers manage it.
hint3: You know what to do without reading any instructions.
hint4: 'No help needed: the app is so ___ my grandma used it straight away.'

hint1: Photographers plan one in every shot.
hint2: In a portrait photo, it is usually the face.
hint3: On a homepage, it might be one huge photo or a bright button.
hint4: The one spot on a screen that you notice before anything else.

hint1: Tiny, curly or faded typefaces make it worse.
hint2: Can you tell a capital I from a small l?
hint3: Doctors' handwriting is famous for having very little of it.
hint4: How easily each single character can be recognised.

hint1: Long walls of words with no breaks hurt it.
hint2: Short sentences and shorter paragraphs help it.
hint3: Lines that run too wide across a screen damage it.
hint4: How pleasant a whole page of writing is to get through.

hint1: Social media companies track it closely.
hint2: Likes, comments and shares on Douyin are signs of it.
hint3: Quizzes, polls and games on a site help to raise it.
hint4: How much visitors stay, click, comment and join in.

hint1: A game has thousands; a printed poster has none.
hint2: Dragging a slider or typing in a box are examples.
hint3: Liking a post or zooming into a photo counts as one.
hint4: Something a visitor does that makes the site change.

hint1: Without it, visitors wonder whether anything happened.
hint2: A spinning wheel while a page loads is one kind.
hint3: A green tick after you send a form gives you this.
hint4: The site's way of saying 'Got it!' after you do something.

hint1: Links and buttons on a laptop usually have one.
hint2: On a touchscreen there is usually no way to trigger it.
hint3: Shopping sites zoom into a product photo when your arrow rests on it.
hint4: A button's look while the arrow floats on it, before you click.

hint1: Getting it wrong can squash or stretch a photo.
hint2: Instagram first allowed only square photos, which have 1:1.
hint3: It compares how far across a picture goes with how far up.
hint4: Most TVs and YouTube videos use 16:9.

hint1: Phone makers boast about it for cameras and screens.
hint2: A low one makes photos look blocky when you zoom in.
hint3: 4K video has much more of it than an old DVD.
hint4: 1920 x 1080 is a common one for laptop screens.

hint1: WeChat usually does it to photos before sending them.
hint2: ZIP and JPEG both use it.
hint3: Too much of it makes pictures blurry and patchy.
hint4: Shrinking a photo's data so it takes up less space.

hint1: Big photos and videos make it longer.
hint2: Many visitors leave if it goes past about three seconds.
hint3: Compressing images is one way to cut it.
hint4: The seconds between clicking a link and the page appearing.

hint1: Designers make one before choosing any colours.
hint2: Grey rectangles stand in for photos, and squiggles for words.
hint3: Like a blueprint for a house, but for a webpage.
hint4: A bare skeleton of a page: where things go, no styling yet.

hint1: Car and phone companies build these before launch.
hint2: You can tap through its screens, but nothing is really saved.
hint3: Made in tools like Figma so people can try a site early.
hint4: An early working sample, made before the real thing.

hint1: It hides in a website's code; most visitors never see it.
hint2: It appears if a picture fails to show.
hint3: Unlike a caption, it's for visitors who can't see the photo.
hint4: 'A golden retriever catching a ball' could be this for a dog photo.

hint1: Most modern sites have two or three of these.
hint2: Shrink a browser window slowly and, at each one, things suddenly jump.
hint3: At 768 pixels across, a full menu might turn into a three-line icon.
hint4: The exact pixel number where a site swaps to its mobile arrangement.

hint1: Large shopping sites and libraries both depend on it.
hint2: Deciding whether 'Trainers' goes under 'Shoes' or under 'Sport'.
hint3: Card sorting with real visitors helps designers plan it.
hint4: How a site's content is grouped and labelled so things are easy to find.

hint1: Designers follow an imagined visitor called 'Lily' through it.
hint2: Its maps often show highs and lows of emotion along the way.
hint3: It may begin with a Douyin advert and end with a review weeks later.
hint4: Everything a visitor goes through on the way to reaching a goal.

hint1: Designers often draw one with boxes and arrows.
hint2: Sign in, choose a seat, pay, get a ticket: that's one.
hint3: Unlike a journey, it covers only the clicks inside one app for one job.
hint4: The planned route of pages a visitor moves through to finish one job.

hint1: Psychologists and designers both study it.
hint2: Remembering a code from one page to type on the next adds to it.
hint3: Too many choices and flashing pop-ups push it up.
hint4: How hard your mind has to work to use an app.

hint1: Good designers give every control a clear one.
hint2: Underlined blue words have it: they invite you to press them.
hint3: A door handle's shape tells your hand to pull: that's this.
hint4: The look of an object that signals how you can use it.

hint1: Apps are full of these moments, though few people notice them.
hint2: Pull down to refresh and a little spinner bounces: that's one.
hint3: Instagram's heart popping red when you like a photo is a famous one.
hint4: A brief response to one single tap, like a switch sliding to 'on'.

hint1: It stops a new app from overwhelming beginners.
hint2: A 'Show more' link under a product description is an example.
hint3: 'Advanced settings' tucked behind one tap is a classic case.
hint4: Showing only the essentials at the start, then the rest when asked.

hint1: Eye-tracking studies measure it.
hint2: One red apple in a bowl of green ones has lots of it.
hint3: A flashing pop-up has far more of it than plain grey text.
hint4: How strongly something pops out because it differs from what surrounds it.

hint1: The phrase comes from printed newspapers.
hint2: Editors put the biggest story in this half of the front page.
hint3: On a website, it's whatever shows when the page first opens.
hint4: Put your best stuff here, before visitors have to swipe down.

hint1: Developers set a special meta tag for it on mobile sites.
hint2: It's much narrower on a phone than on a laptop.
hint3: Resize your browser and it grows or shrinks too.
hint4: The rectangle of the page you can see right now, wherever you've scrolled.

hint1: Accessibility experts always check that a site supports it.
hint2: Some fast typists prefer it to pointing and clicking.
hint3: A glowing outline shows which link you've reached as you move along.
hint4: Getting round a site by pressing Enter, Space and Shift, with no pointer.

hint1: Accessibility checkers give every page a score for it.
hint2: Pale grey writing on white fails this check.
hint3: Black on white gets the top score: 21:1.
hint4: Web guidelines say normal text needs at least 4.5:1.

hint1: Online shops pay experts to improve theirs.
hint2: Good page titles and descriptions help with it.
hint3: It helps a shop appear on page one when people type 'cheap trainers'.
hint4: Tricks for appearing near the top of Bing's list of results.

hint1: Every photo on your phone carries some, out of view.
hint2: A photo's date, place and camera model are examples.
hint3: Search engines read it to learn what a page is about.
hint4: Facts about a file, not what's inside it.

hint1: Shop owners watch this number closely.
hint2: Every new member who registers counts as one.
hint3: If 2 in every 100 visitors pay, its rate is 2%.
hint4: The moment a visitor does what the call to action asked.

hint1: Many web teams now work this way, since most visits come from handheld devices.
hint2: You begin with one narrow column and add more as space grows.
hint3: Laptop and desktop versions come later, built up from the tiniest one.
hint4: Planning for a pocket-sized device before any bigger one.

hint1: Game studios run sessions like this before launch.
hint2: Five people can uncover most of a site's big issues this way.
hint3: Designers sit back silently while real visitors attempt tasks.
hint4: Real people use your prototype while you note what goes wrong.

hint1: Most apps go through dozens of these before launch.
hint2: Designers rarely get it right in one go, so they make many.
hint3: Each new draft, reshaped by feedback from testers, is one.
hint4: One round of 'make it, check it, fix it', ready to go again.

hint1: Creative agencies start every project with one.
hint2: It sets out who the site is for, what it must do and the deadline.
hint3: A bakery owner writes one before hiring someone to build her site.
hint4: The document that tells you exactly what a project must achieve.

hint1: Every real project has several, like it or not.
hint2: A small budget and a two-week deadline are both examples.
hint3: 'The site must work on old phones' is one kind.
hint4: A fence the designer must work inside, such as time or money.
